sections.section_title: Clinical Presentation and Initial Bedside Assessment of Abdominal Masses in Pregnancy
sections.description: This section introduces the patient’s presentation and teaches how to approach a pregnant patient in the second trimester with abdominal pain, pelvic symptoms, and dyspnoea. It emphasizes stabilization, focused history, physical examination, and the importance of recognizing mass effect and pregnancy-specific diagnostic constraints.
subtopics: Case overview: nulliparous woman in her 40s at 21 weeks’ gestation with acute abdominal pain and mild dyspnoea
Pregnancy-specific symptom interpretation: distinguishing obstetric, gastrointestinal, urinary, respiratory, and gynecologic causes
Initial maternal assessment: vital signs, oxygenation, cardiopulmonary evaluation, and exclusion of immediate instability
Abdominal examination in pregnancy: uterine size versus apparent abdominal enlargement, tenderness, palpable masses, and signs of peritonism or ascites
Value of bimanual vaginal examination for pelvic mass localization and relationship to the uterus
Symptom relief measures used in the case: analgesia, positioning, and supportive care
Associated findings during admission: low-grade fever, urinary infection, iron deficiency anaemia, inflammatory markers, and physiologic leukocytosis of pregnancy
How obesity and the gravid uterus complicate physical examination and diagnostic interpretation
Red flags that increase concern in pregnant patients with abdominal masses: worsening pain, dyspnoea from mass effect, fever, torsion, rupture, infection, or possible malignancy

sections.section_title: Imaging Strategy and Differential Diagnosis of Complex Adnexal-Appearing Masses During Pregnancy
sections.description: This section explains the safe and effective diagnostic workup for abdominal and pelvic masses in pregnancy, using this case to illustrate how ultrasound, Doppler, MRI, and selected laboratory tests contribute to localization and characterization. It also teaches why degenerating leiomyomas may mimic ovarian pathology such as endometriomas.
subtopics: Ultrasound as first-line imaging in pregnancy: strengths, limitations, and role of colour Doppler
Case ultrasound findings: two large unilocular cystic lesions, peripheral vascularisation, and apparent continuity of the caudal mass with a posterior myoma
MRI without contrast in pregnancy: indications, safety principles, and why gadolinium is generally avoided
Case MRI findings: thick walls, inhomogeneous fluid, focal solid-appearing components, unclear cleavage planes, and absence of adenopathy
Why large uterine leiomyomas can be misdiagnosed as adnexal masses, especially when pedunculated, posterior, or cystically degenerated
Decidualised endometrioma in pregnancy: imaging features and why it entered the differential diagnosis
Cystic degeneration and torsion of leiomyomas: radiologic and clinical correlates
Role and limitations of tumour markers in pregnancy, especially CA-125 trends across trimesters
Interpretation of this patient’s laboratory profile: mild CA-125 elevation, normal other tumour markers, and the non-diagnostic nature of isolated results
Constructing the differential diagnosis: ovarian endometrioma, adnexal neoplasm, pedunculated leiomyoma, degenerating intramural-subserosal myoma, and other cystic pelvic masses

sections.section_title: Diagnostic Reasoning and Decision to Operate in the Second Trimester
sections.description: This section focuses on clinical reasoning: how the team weighed the uncertain diagnosis against maternal symptoms, fetal considerations, and the risk of complications. It teaches indications for conservative management versus surgery and why the second trimester is often the preferred window when intervention is necessary.
subtopics: Principles of managing pelvic and abdominal masses during pregnancy: expectant versus operative strategies
Why conservative management is usually preferred for leiomyomas during pregnancy
Clinical indications for surgery in pregnancy: persistent pain, dyspnoea from compression, suspected torsion, rupture, infection, or oncologic concern
Case-specific reasons for intervention: worsening symptoms, restrictive mechanics, uncertain origin, risk of future enlargement, and need for conclusive diagnosis
Interpreting mixed evidence: imaging suggestive of endometrioma versus clues supporting uterine origin
How slight CA-125 elevation influenced but did not determine decision-making
Multidisciplinary planning among obstetricians, gynaecologists, surgeons, radiologists, and anaesthesia teams
Why the operation was scheduled in the second trimester and the maternal-fetal risk-benefit framework at 21 weeks
Choice of laparotomy versus laparoscopy: effect of mass size, vascularity, multiplicity, intramural involvement, location, and technical feasibility
Preoperative counselling and informed consent: pregnancy loss, haemorrhage, preterm labour, need to limit procedure, and possible need to defer resection of some lesions

sections.section_title: Operative Findings, Surgical Management, and Perioperative Obstetric Care
sections.description: This section explains what happened in the operating room, highlighting the discrepancy between preoperative impression and final intraoperative diagnosis. It also reviews operative principles for myomectomy in pregnancy, selective resection, fetal monitoring, haemorrhage prevention, and perioperative medication choices.
subtopics: Operative exploration in pregnancy: abdominal entry, assessment of pelvic anatomy, and confirmation of fetal viability
Case intraoperative surprise: upper lesion identified as a huge twisted, leaking, pedunculated cystic leiomyoma rather than an adnexal mass
Pathophysiologic basis of symptoms: torsion, ischaemia, necrosis, leakage, pain, and low-grade fever
Selective myomectomy during pregnancy: rationale for excising the pedunculated cranial mass
Technical principles used in the case: pedicle control, gentle excision, haemostasis, and uterine repair
Reason for leaving the caudal pelvic mass in situ: fixation, likely intramural-subserosal origin, and desire to minimize obstetric risk
Collection of peritoneal fluid for cytology and culture in the setting of diagnostic uncertainty
Maternal-fetal intraoperative precautions: documenting fetal heart activity before, during, and after surgery
Use of progesterone prophylaxis and antibiotics in the perioperative period
Postoperative complications and support: anaemia management, transfusion, iron replacement, and monitoring for pregnancy continuation

sections.section_title: Pregnancy Outcome, Delivery Planning, and Clinical Lessons from Atypical Leiomyomas
sections.description: This final section covers postoperative follow-up, pathology, delivery planning, and the broader lessons of the case. It uses the outcome to teach how fibroid size and location affect mode of delivery, how leiomyomas behave across pregnancy and puerperium, and how to avoid overtreatment while preserving maternal and fetal safety.
subtopics: Histopathology in the case: benign uterine leiomyoma with ischaemic necrosis near the twisted pedicle
Postoperative obstetric surveillance: serial follow-up for fetal growth, amniotic fluid, maternal symptoms, and residual mass assessment
Natural history of leiomyomas in pregnancy and postpartum: non-linear growth, degeneration, and postpartum regression
Case outcome: stable pregnancy after surgery, symptom resolution, and reduction in residual myoma size postpartum
Delivery planning when a residual pelvic myoma obstructs the birth canal
Why elective caesarean section at 37 weeks was chosen in this patient
Implications of prior uterine surgery and residual lower pelvic mass for labour and uterine rupture risk
Maternal and neonatal outcomes and postpartum decision-making regarding deferred additional surgery

Key teaching points: atypical leiomyomas can mimic adnexal masses; imaging and examination must be integrated; tumour markers are limited in pregnancy; operate only for clear indications; and tailor delivery mode to mass size, number, and location
Suggested clinical algorithm for future similar cases: presentation, safe imaging, differential diagnosis, multidisciplinary review, criteria for surgery, and follow-up planning
